title: Capacity Planning with Prometheus
intro: Capacity planning answers 'when do we run out, and how much do we need for the next peak?' before the pager does. Most of it is a few PromQL queries plus the N+1 rule: the service must survive its busiest hour even with one zone or node gone. Queries run through promtool against http://prometheus:9090.

steps.prompt: Which filesystems will fill up within 4 days at their current rate? Use predict_linear over the last 6 hours of node_filesystem_avail_bytes.
steps.explanation: db-01 and logs-02 are on track to run out of disk within 4 days.
steps.why: Alerting on 'will be full in N hours' instead of 'is 90% full' gives time to act, and doesn't page for a disk that sits at 91% forever. This is the standard 'disk will fill' alert in most Prometheus rule sets.

steps.prompt: What was the peak request rate over the last 30 days? Use a subquery: max over time of the 5-minute rate, at 1h resolution.
steps.explanation: The peak was about 18,400 requests per second.
steps.why: Size for peaks, not averages: the busiest hour is when capacity fails. Subqueries ([30d:1h]) evaluate an expression over time. Then add expected growth and known events (a sale, a launch), because last month's peak isn't next month's.

steps.prompt: How much of the cluster's CPU is already promised? Divide total CPU requests by total allocatable CPU.
steps.explanation: 86% of the cluster's CPU is reserved by requests.
steps.why: The scheduler places pods by requests, not actual usage. At 86% requested, losing one node of seven (14% of capacity) leaves pods unschedulable. That's the N+1 test: can the remaining nodes absorb the loss of the largest failure domain?

steps.prompt: Compare with what's actually used: divide the CPU used by containers (rate of container_cpu_usage_seconds_total over 5m) by total CPU requests.
steps.explanation: Pods use only 31% of what they request.
steps.why: Big gaps between requested and used capacity are the largest source of cloud waste at scale. Right-size requests from real usage (the Vertical Pod Autoscaler in recommend mode helps) before buying more nodes. Here the cluster isn't short of CPU; it's over-reserved.

steps.prompt: Pull the daily peak request rate for the last 90 days as a range query, to chart the growth trend (1-day step).
expected_commands: promtool query range --start=$(date -d '90 days ago' +%s) --end=$(date +%s) --step=1d http://prometheus:9090 'max_over_time(sum(rate(http_requests_total[5m]))[1d:1h])'
steps.explanation: Peak traffic grows roughly 10% a month.
steps.why: Growth rate plus lead time decides when to act: if new capacity (hardware, quota increases, reserved instances) takes 6 weeks, you order it when the forecast says you'll run out in 8. That's capacity planning as practised at large companies: forecast, lead time, headroom.
